candidates.label: Angle measures an amount of rotation
candidates.description: An angle is not just a shape between two lines but a measure of how far you rotate from a starting direction.
candidates.failure_mode: Students believe angles can only be between 0 and 180 degrees and cannot conceptualize angles like 270 degrees or negative angles

candidates.label: cos(theta) is the horizontal projection of the radius
candidates.description: cos(theta) represents how far the endpoint of a unit radius sits horizontally from the center.
candidates.failure_mode: Students swap sin and cos in applied problems, using cos for vertical height and sin for horizontal position

candidates.label: sin squared plus cos squared always equals one
candidates.description: Because sin and cos are the y and x coordinates of a point on the unit circle, they always satisfy the Pythagorean relationship.
candidates.failure_mode: Students treat this as an isolated memorized formula rather than recognizing it as the Pythagorean theorem applied directly to the unit circle

candidates.label: Reference angle maps any angle to first quadrant
candidates.description: The reference angle is the acute angle between a terminal side and the nearest x-axis, used to compute trig values in any quadrant.
candidates.failure_mode: Students compute trig values of angles like 150 or 225 degrees from scratch instead of using the reference angle and adjusting only the sign

candidates.label: sin(theta) is the vertical projection of the radius
candidates.description: sin(theta) represents how high the endpoint of a unit radius sits above the center — it is literally a vertical distance.
candidates.failure_mode: Students know sin as opposite over hypotenuse but cannot connect it to the vertical component of a rotating vector, causing failure on circular motion problems like y = 30 + 18 sin(theta)

candidates.label: Unit circle point is (cos theta, sin theta)
candidates.description: On a circle of radius 1, the point reached after rotating by angle theta has x-coordinate equal to cos(theta) and y-coordinate equal to sin(theta).
candidates.failure_mode: Students know sin and cos as triangle ratios but cannot locate them on the unit circle or apply them to angles beyond 90 degrees
